idiom_name: JCE SealedObject/Cipher on the JVM + hand-written toString and JSON codec
implementation_notes: Scala inherits the JVM mechanisms, so the sealed map is a javax.crypto.SealedObject (or Cipher.doFinal bytes) and the transfer object is a class whose protected state is a private field; the language-specific friction is that case classes generate toString, equals, hashCode, copy and unapply over constructor fields, so protected values either stay out of the constructor or the generated rendering has to be overridden by hand, and declarative JSON codecs (circe, zio-json, play-json) serialize only what the codec says - one custom Encoder/Decoder can seal a single field. What replaces the classic structure: the private map plus an overridden toString replaces the class's masked view, and the codec replaces the serialized data map. The crypto itself is platform-supplied.
pitfalls: Case-class product machinery (toString/equals/hashCode/copy/unapply) is generated over constructor parameters: a protected field declared as a parameter is printed, copied and hashed unless every generated method is overridden, so keep sensitive state out of the parameter list.

@transient is a Java-serialization annotation: Scala.js/Native and most JSON codecs ignore it, and a lazy val recomputes after deserialization, so it must not be the only thing keeping a value off the wire.

Scala collections wrapped with asJava/asScala share the underlying data: clearing the Scala mutable map after sealing can leave the wrapped Java view observable, so copy into the sealed structure and drop all references.
Cross-platform code (Scala.js/Scala Native) has no JCE: keep the crypto behind a small facade or the sealed map becomes a JVM-only detail that breaks other targets' builds.
